title: Tu B'Av (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)
hook: six days after the saddest day comes a day of love, when young women danced in the vineyards
tomorrow: Year two close: the whole Torah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eicha, Lamentations read sitting on the floor. Your line was baseless hatred destroys. Did you set one grudge down? Now count six days past the saddest day. Day six hundred ninety-five.

There were no happier days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur. That's the claim, near the end of a tractate of the Mishnah about fasts, in the name of a sage called Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Yom Kippur? The day of not eating, of confessing, of standing all day in white? Happy? And the fifteenth of Av, a quiet date in midsummer, sitting just six days after the day Jerusalem is mourned on the floor. Today, a happy day that comes straight out of grief.
screen: `NO HAPPIER DAYS THAN THESE.` → `YOM KIPPUR? HAPPY?` → `SIX DAYS AFTER THE SADDEST DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tu B'Av means the fifteenth of Av. Hebrew letters are numbers, and fifteen is written tet and vav, nine and six, which together sound like tu. Then the Mishnah tells us what happened. On those two days the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white clothes, and every dress was borrowed. Even the king's daughter borrowed from the high priest's daughter, and the high priest's daughter from the next family down, so that no girl who didn't own a fine dress would be put to shame. Nobody could tell whose family was rich. And they went out and danced in the vineyards, calling to the young men: lift your eyes and see whom you choose. The Mishnah doesn't say why either day was so happy. The Talmud fills that in later. Yom Kippur is easy: it was the day of forgiveness. For Tu B'Av, it collects several reasons. On this day, it says, the tribes were first allowed to marry one another. On this day the tribe of Benjamin, cut off after a terrible civil war in the book of Judges, was let back in. On this day, some say, the generation dying in the wilderness stopped dying. On this day the cutting of wood for the altar ended for the year, as the summer sun weakened. Most of the reasons are about a door opening: between tribes, back into a family, out of a long sentence. The calendar doesn't explain itself, but it does put the two days side by side. First the floor, the candle and the cry of how. Then, six days later, white dresses and dancing. Mourning gets its full day, on the floor, and then the same month turns to white dresses. In Israel today Tu B'Av has come back as a day of love: weddings, flowers, songs on the radio. After mourning, love.
screen: `TET AND VAV: FIFTEEN.` · `EVERY DRESS WAS BORROWED.` · `DANCING IN THE VINEYARDS.` · `A DOOR OPENS.` · then, large: `AFTER MOURNING, LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: celebrate someone you love. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring one person to mind, a partner, a friend, a child, a parent, someone who has stood by you in a hard stretch. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Then think of one thing about them you've never quite said out loud: something they do that makes your life lighter. Let it fill you up for a while. You don't have to send it yet. Just hold the person and the thing together, the way you'd hold a gift before giving it. The bell holds the time.
Tu B'Av. The fifteenth of Av: borrowed white dresses, dancing in the vineyards, and a day of love six days after mourning. Today's word.
Your line: after mourning, love. Today, say the thing out loud, or write it down and send it, to the person you held in mind. Day six hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Tu B'Av, the fifteenth of Av, has no fixed rituals in Jewish law beyond omitting some penitential prayers; in modern Israel it is celebrated as a day of love, popular for weddings, parties and romance.

original.note: Hebrew: the fifteenth of Av. tet is nine, vav is six.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Jewish valentine's day.
what it means: the fifteenth of Av, when Jerusalem's daughters danced in borrowed white, six days after Tisha B'Av.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Taanit closes on it; the Talmud (Taanit 30b–31a) gives the reasons: tribes intermarry, Benjamin returns, the wood-cutting ends.

notes: Mishnah Taanit 4:8 (4:7 in some editions) paraphrased: borrowed white garments, chain of borrowing beginning with the king's daughter, dancing in vineyards, 'lift your eyes and see whom you choose'. Verify.

Talmud Taanit 30b–31a reasons: tribes permitted to intermarry; Benjamin readmitted; the wilderness generation stopped dying; Hoshea ben Elah removed guards; the slain of Betar allowed burial; end of wood-cutting. Only four are named; check selection and wording ('some say' for the wilderness reason).
Number fifteen written tet-vav to avoid yod-heh, a divine name; not stated in the script.
The 'happy because of forgiveness' reason for Yom Kippur is given in the Gemara (giving of the second tablets / forgiveness). Verify.
Modern Israeli Tu B'Av as a day of love is a revival; stated descriptively.

Review pass: teach reworded so the Yom Kippur 'day of forgiveness' reason is attributed to the Talmud, not implied to be in the Mishnah; 'every reason opens a door' softened to 'most', since the end of wood-cutting does not fit that frame. The hook's 'no happier days' line is a paraphrase of Mishnah Taanit 4:8, not a quotation.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut "a date most people have never heard of" and the superlative "the strangest happy day in the calendar"; replaced the stock line "not allowed to be the last word" with a concrete image from the Mishnah.
